verdict.rationale: The lexical pattern across both Testaments presents the human person as a composite of a material constituent and an immaterial constituent, and this primary claim is decisive. Gen 2.7 joins ʿaphar (dust, 110 occurrences) with neshamah (breath, 24 occurrences) and the product is a nephesh chayyah (living being); nephesh recurs 754 times for the whole living self. Matt 10.28 sets soma (body) against psyche as targets of different harm, and 2 Cor 5.8 assumes a self that is at home or away from the soma. Eccl 12.7 names the death-split: dust to earth, ruach to God. The second-tier sub-claim, whether the immaterial side is one principle (dichotomy) or two (trichotomy), is lexically underdetermined. psyche (102 NT occurrences) and pneuma (379) co-occur in only five NT verses, and only 1 Thess 5.23 and Heb 4.12 set them in any partition; in both the grammar reads as well as a whole-person merism as an ontological enumeration, and OT ruach, neshamah, and nephesh interchange freely for the inner life. The proposition itself labels that partition debated and in-house, so the verdict affirms the unity it asserts.

scripture.force: Yahweh forms ʾadam from the ʿaphar (dust) of the ground and breathes nishmat chayyim (breath of life) into his nostrils, and the man becomes a nephesh chayyah (living being). The Hebrew of this verse, confirmed in the OSHB word layer, contains ʿaphar, neshamah, nephesh, and ʾadam but NOT ruach; the material dust and the divine breath combine and the composite product is one living person. nephesh here denotes the whole animate creature, not a detachable inner part, so the verse grounds the material-plus-immaterial unity without by itself establishing any partition within the immaterial side.

Jesus distinguishes those who can kill the soma (accusative singular) but cannot kill the psyche (accusative singular) from the one who can destroy both psyche and soma in gehenna. The MorphGNT parsing shows soma and psyche as two distinct accusative objects of two contrasted verbs, with the soul surviving the killing of the body. This is a clean binary contrast of a material and an immaterial constituent and is the strongest single witness for the primary unity claim.

Paul prefers ekdemesai ek tou somatos (to be away from the body) kai endemesai pros ton kyrion (and at home with the Lord). The genitive tou somatos is the thing departed from, and the continuing personal subject (the we who are confident and prefer) is grammatically distinct from the soma. This supports a two-part constitution: a material body and an immaterial self capable of conscious presence with the Lord apart from the body. It says nothing about a third constituent.

The ʿaphar (dust) returns to the earth as it was and the ruach returns to God who gave it. The OSHB word layer confirms ʿaphar and ruach in this verse. This is a clear binary separation at death: the material constituent to the ground, the immaterial constituent to God. The death pattern names two elements, not three, and so coheres with the dichotomy reading of the immaterial side while still grounding the basic material-immaterial unity.

Paul prays that the God of peace would sanctify the addressees holoteleis (wholly) and that their pneuma kai psyche kai soma be preserved blamelessly. MorphGNT confirms three nominative-singular nouns in series joined by repeated kai, governed by a single adjective holokleron and a third-singular optative verb teretheie. The singular adjective and singular verb governing the triple subject are the lexical hook that lets the line be read as an exhaustive whole-person prayer (a merism) just as readily as a list of three ontological parts. The grammar does not rank the two readings.

The logos of God pierces achri merismou psyches kai pneumatos, harmon te kai myelon. MorphGNT shows merismou (genitive, dividing) governing psyche and pneuma (both genitive singular) in parallel with harmon and myelon (joints and marrow, genitive plural). Because the soul-spirit pair stands in the same construction as the physical joints-and-marrow pair, the genitives are genuinely ambiguous: they can be partitive (the word divides soul from spirit) or objective (the word penetrates through the whole interior, soul and spirit alike). The verse asserts the penetrating discernment of the word, and the construction by itself does not settle whether psyche and pneuma are separable constituents.

As her nephesh was departing, for she was dying, Rachel named her son. The OSHB word layer confirms nephesh in this verse alongside the dying-and-departing language. Here nephesh is the life or self that leaves the body at death, the same immaterial referent that elsewhere is carried by ruach (Eccl 12.7). This in-canon interchange of nephesh and ruach for the departing inner person is exactly why the words do not cleanly rank a two-part versus three-part immaterial constitution.

All in whose nostrils was nishmat-ruach chayyim died in the flood. The OSHB word layer confirms both neshamah and ruach in this verse, standing together in construct as the breath-of-spirit-of-life. The two terms here function as overlapping near-synonyms for the one life-breath rather than as two discrete substances, which complicates any clean lexical separation of the immaterial into ranked parts.

As long as my neshamah is in me and the ruach of Eloah is in my nostrils, Job swears. The OSHB word layer confirms neshamah and ruach in this verse, set in a tight poetic couplet where both denote the divinely given life-breath within the speaker. The two Hebrew terms function as near-synonyms in this line, reinforcing that lexical labels alone cannot fix how many immaterial constituents the person has.

Paul contrasts the psychikos anthropos (natural person, psychikos occurs 6 times in the NT) with the pneumatikos (spiritual person, pneumatikos 26 times) regarding receptivity to the things of the Spirit of God. The adjectival contrast describes two modes of human existence relative to God rather than two substances inside one human, so it does not by itself establish a trichotomous ontology; here pneuma language points to the Spirit and to the person under the Spirit, not to a third part of the self.

complicating_texts.resolution: The psychikos and pneumatikos contrast describes modes of relating to God, not separable substances. pneuma here points to the Holy Spirit and pneumatikos to the person under the Spirit, so the verse does not require a trichotomous ontology. It complicates a strict three-part reading but leaves the basic material-immaterial unity untouched.

Genesis 7.22 places neshamah and ruach in construct with one another, which undercuts a clean lexical separation of the two as independent constituents. The resolution is that OT vocabulary for the immaterial shows overlapping ranges. This is internal to the dichotomy-trichotomy sub-question and supports its disputed status rather than the primary unity claim.

Job uses neshamah and ruach in a synonymous poetic couplet, confirming that Hebrew can treat these as near-synonyms. This shows lexical labels alone cannot settle the dichotomy-trichotomy sub-question; it does not weaken the material-immaterial unity, which Matt 10.28 and 2 Cor 5.8 carry independently.

Genesis 35.18 uses nephesh for the life or self that departs at death, the same role Ecclesiastes 12.7 assigns to ruach. nephesh and ruach therefore overlap as labels for the departing inner person. This interchange is the core reason the vocabulary does not rank a two-part versus three-part immaterial constitution, so the complication stands as a feature of the underdetermined sub-question.

variants.note: None of the anchor verses lie in the ingested ECM window (3 John 1.1 to 1.15), so no CBGM apparatus was consulted; this is not_in_ecm_scope honestly. No textual variant in Gen 2.7, Matt 10.28, 2 Cor 5.8, 1 Thess 5.23, or Heb 4.12 alters the constitutional vocabulary (nephesh, neshamah, ruach, soma, psyche, pneuma). The pneuma kai psyche kai soma series of 1 Thess 5.23 and the psyches kai pneumatos pairing of Heb 4.12 are stable across the manuscript tradition, so the verdict holds across plausible readings.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads psyche and pneuma as overlapping labels for the single immaterial aspect, supported by their co-occurrence in only five NT verses and by the free OT interchange of nephesh, neshamah, and ruach (Gen 7.22, Job 27.3, Gen 35.18, Eccl 12.7). Takes 1 Thess 5.23 as an exhaustive whole-person prayer governed by singular holokleron and a singular verb, and Heb 4.12 as parallel with joints-and-marrow describing total penetration. Treats Matt 10.28 and 2 Cor 5.8 as the paradigm body-soul binary. This is the strongest case that the immaterial side is one principle.

Reads the deliberate three-term series pneuma kai psyche kai soma in 1 Thess 5.23 and the explicit merismos psyches kai pneumatos in Heb 4.12 as load-bearing distinctions, taking pneuma as the God-conscious faculty and psyche as the seat of natural personality and life. Points out that Paul chose to name three items, not two, in a careful benediction, and that Heb 4.12 says the word can divide soul and spirit at all. This is the strongest case that the immaterial side carries two distinguishable principles.

Reads Gen 2.7 nephesh chayyah as the whole living person rather than a soul installed in a body, and notes nephesh denotes the entire animate self across its 754 occurrences. Takes the body-immaterial split at death (Eccl 12.7, 2 Cor 5.8) as real but resists hard substance dualism, treating psyche and pneuma functionally. This lens grants the unity claim while cautioning that the words describe one living person more than an assembly of parts.

hermeneutics.notes: The lexical pattern lands the primary claim of a material-and-immaterial unity with strength: dense, pan-canonical, grammatically clear in Matt 10.28 and 2 Cor 5.8. The internal dichotomy-versus-trichotomy question is genuinely underdetermined by lexicon alone, because psyche and pneuma co-occur in only five NT verses and only two of those set them in any partition, while the OT terms nephesh, neshamah, and ruach interchange freely for the inner person. The competing lenses are stated symmetrically and each in its strongest form.

stem_audit.notes: The stem encodes the disputed status of the dichotomy-trichotomy partition as in-house, which mirrors the lexical situation rather than preloading a verdict; it does not assert which partition is correct. The load-bearing assertion is the material-immaterial unity, and that is independently testable against Gen 2.7, Matt 10.28, 2 Cor 5.8, and Eccl 12.7, so it is not preloaded. Verdict unchanged from the prior file: affirms remains true. The enrichment grounds the counts in real queried data (OSHB word layer for Hebrew, MorphGNT for Greek) and adds the decisive co-occurrence finding that psyche and pneuma share only five NT verses.

lay_summary: The Bible steadily portrays a human person as a unity of a material body and an immaterial life. In Genesis 2.7 the LORD forms the man from the dust of the ground and breathes the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man becomes a living being. Two ingredients combine and the result is one living person. Jesus in Matthew 10.28 separates those who can kill the body from the one who can destroy both soul and body, which assumes the soul outlasts the killing of the body. Paul in 2 Corinthians 5.8 speaks of being away from the body and at home with the Lord, again a self that continues when the body is left. Ecclesiastes 12.7 states the death pattern: the dust returns to the earth and the spirit returns to God who gave it. Two parts, plainly. Whether the immaterial side is one principle or two is much harder to settle from the words alone, and that is where readers diverge. The two key Greek words, soul and spirit, appear together in only five verses of the whole New Testament, and only First Thessalonians 5.23 (spirit, soul, and body) and Hebrews 4.12 (the word dividing soul and spirit) set them side by side at all. In First Thessalonians the three words sit under one singular adjective and one singular verb, so the line reads just as well as a prayer for the whole person as a list of three parts. In Hebrews soul and spirit stand in the same grammar as joints and marrow, so the sentence may mean the word divides soul from spirit, or simply that it pierces the deepest interior. Meanwhile the Hebrew words for breath, spirit, and soul trade places freely, as when the soul departs at death in Genesis 35.18 but the spirit departs in Ecclesiastes 12.7. So the vocabulary firmly supports the body and immaterial-life unity, but it does not rank the two-part and three-part readings of the inner side, which is why that question stays open and in-house.
